Subject: Egress connectivity evaluation: interface endpoints vs VPC peering vs S2S tunnel for FinServe private deploy

Team —

FinServe is getting urgent about the private deployment path for their inference cluster (regional US-east). They have two high-level constraints we need to balance:

- Zero-trust egress (no public internet paths for model inference traffic) and strong auditability for SOC2/PCI reviews.
- Predictable latency under 40ms p95 for token generation (their SLA ask).

I pulled together a short matrix and attached our recent latency runs + cost sketch. High level options: interface endpoints (PrivateLink-style, vendor-managed interface endpoints), VPC peering (direct L3 route), or a site-to-site encrypted tunnel (IPsec/MPLS).

Questions for the group:
- From an operational perspective which option minimizes blast radius and simplifies troubleshooting?
- Which option best maps to FinServe's compliance ask (no shared public egress, audited flows)?
- Any blockers for their network team (NAT, overlapping CIDRs, egress inspection) we should call out now?

Can each of you reply with 1) a short pro/con list, 2) any immediate red flags, and 3) an estimated implementation timeline (weeks) for pilot. I'll consolidate and send to Carlos + Alex.

Thanks —

Short take — I'll keep it tactical:

1) Interface endpoints (Redwood-hosted ENIs / AWS Interface Endpoints)
   - Pros: Strong isolation (no routed L3 into customer VPC), per-endpoint IAM + security groups, traffic never traverses public internet. Easy to scale per-region. Auditing at endpoint + flow logs is straightforward.
   - Cons: Higher per-hour cost on endpoint/ENI, potential hotspot if we have many customer VPCs; cross-account endpoint plumbing and limits can be annoying. Latency: typically low but a function of AZ locality; our microbench shows p95 ~ 15–35ms depending on AZ pairing (see latency-tests-privatedeploy.csv).
   - Pilot time: 2–3 weeks (prod-like test with FinServe test VPC + one AZ pairing).

2) VPC Peering
   - Pros: Simple L3 routing, low steady-state cost, minimal per-connection overhead. Very low network latency if in same region.
   - Cons: CIDR overlap is a show-stopper for many banks. Peering is flat L3; harder to enforce fine-grained egress controls on specific subpaths. Troubleshooting cross-account routes can be more manual. Not ideal if FinServe needs explicit per-tenant isolation.
   - Pilot time: 1–2 weeks for a limited peering test, longer if route tables/nat/proxy changes required.

3) Site-to-site tunnel (IPsec/MPLS)
   - Pros: Fits existing FinServe security model (they operate MPLS appliances), auditable and can be forced through their appliances. Good when CIDRs overlap and they insist on on-prem control.
   - Cons: Higher ops overhead, introduces a third-party device in path (break-fix longer), and can add variable latency (we saw p95 spikes to 60–120ms under load in prior MPLS tunnels). Cost skew depends on their network vendor.
   - Pilot time: 3–6 weeks (coord across netops, firewall rules, certs, testing).

Immediate red flags: FinServe's initial questionnaire listed overlapping CIDRs in their corp VPC and said they want per-service audit logs retained 12 months (we need to size flow logs retention). If overlaps are true, peering is off the table unless they re-IP.

Happy to run a quick traceroute matrix once they confirm VPC CIDRs.

Adding the compliance lens (SOC 2 / PCI flavors):

- Private endpoints (interface) are attractive because we can provide both flow-level logs (VPC flow logs / ENI-level metrics) and application logs. That maps well to evidence collection for access controls and network segmentation (CC6.1 style controls).
- For VPC peering, auditors often push back on lack of strict per-application gateways; routing alone is considered weaker than explicit endpoint enforcement. You can add an inspection hop but that increases complexity.
- S2S tunnels with customer-managed appliances are audit-friendly but you must ensure key rotation, monitoring, and that we capture both sides of flow logs (ours + customer's). Also check egress rules — some banks require TLS termination inside their network (we must avoid terminating TLS on our side unless explicitly allowed).

Operational asks for FinServe before we commit:
1) Confirm CIDR map (include overlapping subnets).
2) Desired retention and format for flow logs / flow samples.
3) Any SSL/TLS interception policies on their end — that affects how we present certs.

I'll volunteer to assemble an evidence checklist and a minimal audit runbook (I can have a draft in 4 business days).

-Kimberly

Hi all — quick vendor-side notes from NetSecure (we're the managed connectivity partner FinServe sometimes uses):

- Interface endpoint model is fast to stitch and our team can provision endpoint interfaces and assign private DNS in <48 hours once accounts are authorized. Costs are predictable; NetSecure passes through AWS endpoint hourly charges + a small management fee. Latency wise we expect <30ms p95 if endpoints are in same AZ pairing.
- Peering is the cheapest but we commonly see customers accidentally expose broader CIDRs unless route tables are carefully curated. We can script route table validators but this is a common human error area.
- For S2S tunnels we offer a managed IPsec headend that terminates on our backbone (MPLS/EW) and hands over to customer appliance. SLA for latency stability depends on the carrier path — we can commit to 99.9% link availability but not to p95 latency under heavy inference loads without additional bandwidth reservation.

Estimate for a pilot (NetSecure helps implement):
- Interface endpoint pilot: 1 week (provision endpoints, run test harness).
- Controlled peering test: 4–5 days (includes route validators).
- S2S tunnel pilot: 2–3 weeks (depending on firewall change windows).

I'll attach a quick implementation checklist in the Drive link; happy to run the pilot with FinServe next week if they can provide CIDR & contact for netops.

Thanks everyone — good input. Quick summary and recommended pilot approach: 

Summary:
- If FinServe can re-IP or confirm no overlapping CIDRs, VPC peering gives the lowest steady-state latency and cost, but it lacks fine-grained endpoint enforcement and is riskier from an audit perspective.
- Interface endpoints (PrivateLink-style) are our recommended default for FinServe when they require strict auditability and want Redwood to own the service plane; costs are higher but trade off for simpler evidence collection and per-endpoint controls.
- S2S tunnels are the fall-back for customers that need on-prem termination or have non-negotiable appliance chains; expect longer lead time and more variable latency.

Recommended pilot plan (proposed next steps):
1) FinServe to provide: a) VPC and on-prem CIDR map, b) primary netops contact, c) expected flow-log retention window. (Action: Carlos — can you provide this by EOD Friday?)
2) We run an interface-endpoint pilot in a single AZ pairing (Ben + NetSecure) to validate p95 latency and log collection. (Owner: Ben / Alex; target: 1 week from kickoff)
3) If FinServe confirms no CIDR overlaps, run a narrow peering test to validate route behavior and real-world p95 delta (Owner: Ben / Sean; target: 2–3 business days).
4) Kimberly will prepare an evidence checklist for auditor review during pilot. (Owner: Kimberly; target: 4 business days)

Carlos — if you prefer a site-to-site-first approach given internal appliance requirements, tell us and we'll pivot the timeline. Otherwise we'll plan to kick off the interface endpoint pilot once we have the CIDR map.

Attachments: latency-tests-privatedeploy.csv (benchmarks), mpls-vs-vpn-cost.xlsx (cost sketch), egress-attack-surface-checklist.pdf (security notes).
